card.chief_complaint: dark urine and elevated creatinine after prolonged time on floor

ask.changes_what: Positive → CK, creatinine, potassium, urinalysis; start IV fluids; assess compartments. Negative → still send CK if found down, post-seizure or toxin-exposed.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not exclude rhabdomyolysis by history in obtunded, intoxicated or found-down patients — send CK.
ask.escalation_warning: Tense painful compartment, hyperkalemia or rising creatinine → urgent surgical and nephrology involvement.
ask.how: Ask about muscle pain, weakness, swelling and dark tea/cola-coloured urine, and exposures: found down/prolonged immobilization, seizure, extreme exertion or heat, crush or trauma, cocaine/amphetamines, alcohol, statins/fibrates, antipsychotics (NMS), recent infection. Palpate for tender, swollen or tense muscle compartments and check distal pulses and sensation.
ask.negative_finding: Absent muscle symptoms or dark urine do not exclude rhabdomyolysis; many cases are oligosymptomatic and even qualitative urine myoglobin was positive in only 19% of 475 inpatients (PMID 16267412, Abstract). Measure CK whenever risk factors exist.
ask.pitfalls: Dark urine also comes from hematuria, hemoglobinuria or bilirubin. In 60% of cases multiple causes co-exist and toxins account for 46% (PMID 16267412, Abstract); CK peaks at 24–72 h, so an early value may be modest (unverified recall).
ask.positive_finding: Myalgia or weakness with dark urine after immobilization, exertion, seizure or toxin exposure strongly suggests rhabdomyolysis; check CK and a urine dipstick (heme-positive without red cells).
ask.prerequisites: Collateral history for obtunded or intoxicated patients; medication and drug-use review.
ask.rationale: History of muscle pain, weakness, and dark urine directly supports or refutes rhabdomyolysis as the cause of AKI after prolonged immobilization.
ask.title: Muscle pain/weakness, prolonged immobilization or exertion, dark cola-colored urine

ask.changes_what: A positive exposure history should lead to stopping or dose-adjusting the agent, avoiding further nephrotoxins and monitoring creatinine; still assess obstruction and volume status.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not attribute AKI solely to a drug or contrast when there is oliguria, sepsis, hypotension or possible obstruction; these still need evaluation.
ask.escalation_warning: AKI with hyperkalemia, acidosis, fluid overload or uremic symptoms needs urgent nephrology review regardless of the exposure history.
ask.how: Reconcile all drugs against the chart and pharmacy record, including over-the-counter NSAIDs and herbal products: NSAIDs, ACEi/ARB, diuretics, aminoglycosides, vancomycin (with piperacillin-tazobactam), PPIs, and any iodinated contrast. For each, record start date, dose change and timing relative to the creatinine rise.
ask.negative_finding: No exposure lowers the likelihood of drug-related AKI and contrast nephropathy, redirecting attention to hypovolemia, sepsis, obstruction and intrinsic renal disease.
ask.pitfalls: Patients under-report OTC NSAIDs; PPI-associated AIN can begin weeks to months after the start; contrast-associated AKI is often confounded by the illness that prompted imaging, so timing alone does not prove causation.
ask.positive_finding: A nephrotoxin started or dosed within days of the creatinine rise, or contrast within 48-72 h, makes drug-induced AKI (hemodynamic, ATN or AIN) a leading candidate and identifies an immediately reversible factor.
ask.prerequisites: Access to medication administration and imaging records; collateral history for patients who cannot report OTC use.
ask.rationale: Recent nephrotoxin or contrast exposure could point to a drug-induced or contrast-induced AKI, which would change management.
ask.title: Nephrotoxin and contrast exposure history (NSAID, ACEi/ARB, diuretic, aminoglycoside, vancomycin, PPI, iodinated contrast; timing)

examine.changes_what: Moist membranes and an unfurrowed tongue lower the probability of hypovolemia; dry findings support a fluid trial and checking electrolytes, BUN/creatinine.
examine.do_not_use_when: Not validated for blood loss; do not use these signs to exclude hemorrhagic hypovolemia or shock.
examine.escalation_warning: Hypotension, severe postural dizziness or a postural pulse increment of 30/min or more indicates large volume loss and needs urgent resuscitation regardless of mucosal findings.

evidence.citation: McGee S, Abernethy WB, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient hypovolemic? JAMA. 1999;281(11):1022-1029.
evidence.population: Adults (largely elderly) presenting with suspected hypovolemia due to vomiting, diarrhea or decreased oral intake
evidence.quote: moist mucous membranes and a tongue without furrows argue against it (negative likelihood ratio, 0.3; 95% CI, 0.1-0.6 for both findings)
evidence.reference_standard: Laboratory/clinical criteria for hypovolemia used by the included primary studies; details not visible in abstract
evidence.target_condition: Hypovolemia (dehydration) in adults with vomiting, diarrhea or decreased oral intake - finding: dry oral mucous membranes (LR- is for moist membranes)

evidence.citation: McGee S, Abernethy WB, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient hypovolemic? JAMA. 1999;281(11):1022-1029.
evidence.population: Adults (largely elderly) presenting with suspected hypovolemia due to vomiting, diarrhea or decreased oral intake
evidence.quote: moist mucous membranes and a tongue without furrows argue against it (negative likelihood ratio, 0.3; 95% CI, 0.1-0.6 for both findings)
evidence.reference_standard: Laboratory/clinical criteria for hypovolemia used by the included primary studies; details not visible in abstract
evidence.target_condition: Hypovolemia (dehydration) in adults with vomiting, diarrhea or decreased oral intake - finding: longitudinal tongue furrows (LR- is for tongue without furrows)

examine.how: Inspect the mouth with a light: look at the buccal mucosa and under the tongue for moisture, and at the dorsum of the tongue for longitudinal furrows. Inspect the eyes for sunken globes. Palpate the axilla for sweat. Record each sign separately rather than a global impression.
examine.negative_finding: Moist mucous membranes or a tongue without furrows argue against hypovolemia (LR- 0.3 for either), which is the more useful direction of these signs.
examine.pitfalls: Mouth breathing, oxygen therapy, anticholinergics and age-related changes dry the mouth without volume depletion; sunken eyes and tongue furrows are chronic in many elderly patients.
examine.positive_finding: Dry mucous membranes, furrowed tongue, sunken eyes or a dry axilla each support hypovolemia in patients with vomiting, diarrhea or poor intake; the pooled RCE gives LR+ 2.8 for dry axilla only.
examine.prerequisites: Patient not mouth-breathing on oxygen for a prolonged period and no recent oral intake or mouth care; good lighting.
examine.rationale: Dry mucous membranes help identify hypovolemia as a contributor to AKI, which would prompt a fluid trial.
examine.title: Dry oral mucous membranes, tongue furrows, sunken eyes, dry axilla

examine.changes_what: Positive → catheterize/measure PVR now and seek the cause (drugs, prostate, cauda equina); negative with risk factors → bladder scan.
examine.contraindications: Avoid deep palpation over fresh lower abdominal incisions.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use an absent suprapubic mass to exclude retention in AKI, delirium or suspected cauda equina — measure post-void residual.
examine.escalation_warning: Retention with new saddle anesthesia, leg weakness or back pain → emergent cauda equina evaluation (MRI).
examine.how: Patient supine: percuss from the umbilicus toward the pubis for a dome of suprapubic dullness and palpate for a smooth, tense, tender midline mass rising from the pelvis that provokes urge. Ask about LUTS, straining, dribbling, hematuria, prostate disease, anticholinergic/opioid use and time since last void; confirm with bladder scan or catheter volume.
examine.negative_finding: A non-palpable bladder does not exclude retention: obesity, smaller volumes and silent postoperative or opioid-related distension are missed. Obtain a bladder scan or post-void residual when retention is plausible.
examine.pitfalls: Postoperative bladder volume >500 mL was present in 44% at recovery-room discharge, and 54% of those without symptoms of distension could not void within 30 min (PMID 14977795, Abstract). Pelvic masses, pregnancy and ascites mimic; palpation cannot estimate volume.
examine.positive_finding: A palpable or percussible bladder above the pubis with inability to void indicates retention — catheterize and measure volume. This is a treatable cause of AKI, delirium and abdominal pain.
examine.prerequisites: Attempt to void first when able; know time of last void.
examine.rationale: Palpating for a distended bladder can quickly identify urinary retention as a reversible cause of AKI.
examine.title: Suprapubic palpation / percussion for distended bladder; LUTS and prostate history

examine.changes_what: Positive postural increment: treat as significant hypovolemia/hemorrhage; resting tachycardia: prompts search for cause (PE, tamponade, sepsis, bleeding) rather than a specific diagnosis.
examine.contraindications: Do not stand a patient who is hypotensive, has suspected hip/spine fracture, or is at high fall risk.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not perform postural measurements in hypotensive, syncopal, or fall-prone patients; do not use resting heart rate alone to exclude hemorrhage in beta-blocked or elderly patients.
examine.escalation_warning: Tachycardia with hypotension, elevated JVP, or pulsus paradoxus suggests tamponade or massive PE; with fever suggests sepsis - escalate immediately.

evidence.citation: Roy CL, Minor MA, Brookhart MA, Choudhry NK. Does this patient with a pericardial effusion have cardiac tamponade? JAMA. 2007;297(16):1810-8.
evidence.population: Pooled studies of patients with known tamponade or referred for pericardiocentesis with known effusion (8 studies)
evidence.reference_standard: Echocardiographic/hemodynamic diagnosis of tamponade (varied by study)
evidence.target_condition: Cardiac tamponade among patients with known pericardial effusion (tachycardia present)

evidence.citation: McGee S, Abernethy WB, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient hypovolemic? JAMA. 1999;281(11):1022-9.
evidence.population: Healthy adult volunteers undergoing phlebotomy (pooled from 10 studies of postural vital signs; large blood loss category)
evidence.quote: a much greater sensitivity for large blood loss of 97% (95% CI, 91%-100%); the corresponding specificity is 98% (95% CI, 97%-99%)
evidence.reference_standard: Known volume of phlebotomy (large blood loss as defined by the review)
evidence.target_condition: COMPOSITE: severe postural dizziness OR postural pulse increment >=30/min, for large blood loss (phlebotomy)

evidence.citation: McGee S, Abernethy WB, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient hypovolemic? JAMA. 1999;281(11):1022-9.
evidence.population: Healthy adult volunteers undergoing phlebotomy (moderate blood loss category)
evidence.quote: The presence of either finding has a sensitivity for moderate blood loss of only 22% (95% confidence interval [CI], 6%-48%)
evidence.reference_standard: Known volume of phlebotomy (moderate blood loss as defined by the review)
evidence.target_condition: COMPOSITE: severe postural dizziness OR postural pulse increment >=30/min, for moderate blood loss (phlebotomy)

examine.how: Count the radial or apical pulse for 30-60 s after at least 2 minutes at rest (supine); tachycardia is >100/min. For the postural component, keep the patient supine 2 minutes, then standing 1 minute, and record the pulse rise; a rise of 30/min or more, or inability to stand because of dizziness, is positive.
examine.negative_finding: Supine tachycardia is frequently absent after moderate blood loss, so a normal resting rate does not exclude hypovolemia; a normal postural pulse response has modest value after moderate blood loss (composite sensitivity 22%).
examine.pitfalls: Beta-blockers, pacing, athletic training, and autonomic neuropathy blunt tachycardia; fever, pain, anxiety, and drugs cause tachycardia without hypovolemia; the postural test is unsafe in unstable patients.
examine.positive_finding: A large postural pulse increment (>=30/min) or severe postural dizziness is highly specific for large-volume blood loss; resting tachycardia is present in about three-quarters of patients with cardiac tamponade but is nonspecific across shock, PE, sepsis, anemia, and thyrotoxicosis.
examine.prerequisites: Patient rested; note beta-blockers, pacemaker, and pain/anxiety.
examine.rationale: Resting tachycardia may indicate hypovolemia or ongoing systemic stress, guiding urgency and resuscitation.
examine.title: Resting heart rate >100/min (and postural pulse increment)
